484.title: The lowest of all
484.hook: whoever knows himself lowest of all is counted highest (Sukhmani 12)
484.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's years of carrying water for Guru Angad as a model of seva, and in gurdwaras today volunteers wash dishes, sweep and mind shoes, often without anyone knowing their names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahankaar: pride of power, of youth, of wealth, even of good deeds, and every pedestal has a drop. Today the same ashtpadi turns the ladder upside down.

Sikh tradition tells of an old man who carried water. Every morning before dawn, for years, he walked to the river, filled a pitcher, and brought it back for his teacher, Guru Angad, to bathe. One dark, stormy morning he tripped near a weaver's house and fell into the pit where the loom stood. The weaver's wife heard the noise and said, more or less: that's only Amru, the man with no home, who wanders around after his guru. A nobody. That nobody became the third Guru, Guru Amar Das.
screen: `AN OLD MAN CARRIES WATER.` → `HE FALLS. ONLY AMRU, A NOBODY.` → `THE NOBODY BECOMES THE THIRD GURU.`

segments.voice: Later in the twelfth ashtpadi, after the prides have been named, Guru Arjan turns the ladder over. Aapas kau jo jaanai neechaa, sou ganeeai sabh te oochaa. Whoever knows himself to be low is counted the highest of all. Neechaa: low, beneath. Oochaa: high, above. Ordinary Punjabi, words for a shelf or a hill. The verb in the middle matters: ganeeai, is counted, is reckoned. The line doesn't say the humble person feels high, or gets promoted at work. It says that in the real reckoning, God's count, the order is reversed. The next line deepens it: the one whose mind becomes the dust of all recognizes the Name in every heart. That's why the low place works: when you're not looking down on anyone, you can finally see what's in them. Back to the story. Tradition says when Guru Angad heard what the weaver's wife had called Amar Das, the homeless one, he called him the home of the homeless. The insult became a title. Tradition says Amar Das was already an old man when he became Guru, and asked everyone who came to see him, even, in the story, the emperor Akbar, to eat first in the langar, in the same rows as everyone else. The lowest seat, made into the door. So this isn't a trick for getting ahead. The stanza describes how things are already counted. We just can't see the scoreboard.
screen: `NEECHAA: LOW. OOCHAA: HIGH.` · `COUNTED, NOT FELT.` · `THE DUST OF ALL SEES EVERY HEART.` · `HOME OF THE HOMELESS.` · then, large: `LOWEST IS HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose day you could make easier, a roommate, a coworker, someone at home, and one small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: the dishes, a refilled water jug, a door held. Picture yourself doing it and walking away without a word, and let that feel like enough.
Neechaa, low, beneath. Whoever knows himself neechaa is counted highest, the way an old water carrier became the third Guru.
Your line: lowest is highest. The homeless one became the home of the homeless. More tomorrow.

485.title: Living ashtpadi 12
485.hook: humility is the doorway to every virtue in Sukhmani
485.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the twelfth ashtpadi's warnings about the I that claims to be the doer, and in many gurdwaras Asa di Var, with its line on sweetness and humility, is sung each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neechaa: whoever knows himself low is counted highest, like the water carrier who became the third Guru. Today we close the twelfth ashtpadi by living it.

Two words, said badly or said well, can change a whole evening: I'm sorry. Most of us know exactly how hard they are. You rehearse them in the car. You add a but. You explain why it wasn't really your fault before you reach the part where it was. The apology gets stuck somewhere between the throat and the pride. And when someone finally says it plainly, no but, no speech, something in the room loosens. Sukhmani has spent a whole ashtpadi on why.
screen: `I'M SORRY. TWO WORDS.` → `REHEARSED, STUCK, WITH A BUT.` → `SAID PLAINLY, THE ROOM LOOSENS.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is twenty-four ashtpadis long, and the twelfth lands near the middle. Before it, Guru Arjan has talked about remembering the Name, the company of the holy, the One who does everything. Here he names what all of that depends on. In the second stanza, in paraphrase: as long as a person thinks, something gets done by me, there's no peace for them. As long as they think, I am the doer, they keep going round and round. The I is the blockage; while it stands in the doorway, nothing else comes through. That's why many Sikhs call humility the doorway to the other virtues. Guru Nanak had already said something like it in Asa di Var, a hymn sung in many gurdwaras every morning: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtue and goodness. Mithat neevee, in Punjabi. Sweetness, and lowness. Notice the pair. Humility in Sikh teaching is never sour, never a grim, hunched-over feeling of being nothing. It's sweet: easy to be around, quick to laugh, quick to say sorry. An apology is humility in its smallest size. It says: I was the doer of this, and it wasn't right. Owning the mistake is the opposite of pride, because pride's whole job is to defend the self. So the twelfth ashtpadi lands somewhere very ordinary: a kitchen, a car, a group chat, wherever two people have rubbed each other the wrong way. Humility first, and then everything else has room.
screen: `THE MIDDLE OF SUKHMANI.` · `WHILE I AM THE DOER, NO PEACE.` · `MITHAT NEEVEE: SWEET AND LOW.` · `SORRY: HUMILITY, SMALL SIZE.` · then, large: `HUMILITY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let the past week drift by, a sharp word, a late reply, a promise that slipped, and without hunting for big guilt, look for one small thing where you were the doer and it wasn't right. When you find it, say the words silently and plainly, with no but on the end: I'm sorry. Feel how short the sentence is.
Mithat neevee, sweetness and lowness. Humility as the doorway: while I am the doer blocks it, nothing else comes through.
Your line: humility first. Sweet, and low, and quick to say sorry. That's day four hundred eighty-five, done.

486.title: Ashtpadi 13, salok: the holy
486.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach the thirteenth ashtpadi's salok on the sant, and Sikh life places great weight on sangat, the company of the good, in shared prayer, singing and the langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mithat neevee, sweetness and lowness: humility first, and then everything else has room. Today, a new ashtpadi, the thirteenth.

Who's the best person you actually know? Not the most famous, not the most impressive. The best. Maybe a neighbor who shovels the whole block's sidewalks and never mentions it. An aunt who remembers every birthday. A nurse who stayed after her shift. Now the harder question: have you ever told them? Applause is easy to give a stranger on a stage. It's oddly hard to give the neighbor with the shovel. The salok of the thirteenth ashtpadi starts right there: with the good ones, and what it means to stand near them.
screen: `THE BEST PERSON YOU KNOW.` → `NOT FAMOUS. GOOD.` → `HAVE YOU EVER TOLD THEM?`

segments.voice: The salok's two lines pull in opposite directions. The first, in paraphrase: whoever takes shelter with the saints is carried across. The second: whoever slanders the saints, Nanak, is born again and again. Today we stay with the first; tomorrow the ashtpadi turns to the second, and stays there a long time. First, the word. Sant is usually translated saint, but careful: in the Guru Granth Sahib it isn't a rank anyone hands out. It describes a person whose life is soaked in remembering God: honest, humble, kind, steady. Sukhmani has described such people already, the holy company and the God-conscious one. They might run a shop. They might be your grandmother. Next, the verb: saran, shelter, refuge, the way you'd step under an awning when it rains. The salok isn't asking you to worship good people. It says nearness to them changes you. Sikhs call it sangat, the company, and Sikh worship gathers around it: praying together, singing together, eating together in the langar. Goodness, in this picture, is catching. Stand near it long enough and some of it rubs off, the way a cloth takes on the scent of the flowers it's wrapped around. And the second line hangs over the first like a cloud: if nearness lifts you, contempt for the good drags you down. That's tomorrow. Today: notice the good people, and honor them.
screen: `TWO LINES, OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS.` · `SANT: A LIFE SOAKED IN THE NAME.` · `SARAN: SHELTER UNDER AN AWNING.` · `GOODNESS IS CATCHING.` · then, large: `HONOR THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose goodness is quiet, see their face, and remember one specific thing they did; a small one is best. Hold it there and let yourself be grateful that people like this exist, picturing, if you like, telling them so in one plain sentence. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Sant, a holy person. Soaked in remembering God; shelter near such people, the salok says, carries you across.
Your line: honor the good. Goodness is catching, like scent on a cloth. See you tomorrow.

487.title: The harm of slander
487.hook: slandering the holy spoils the slanderer's own life (Sukhmani 13)
487.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the thirteenth ashtpadi's repeated lines beginning sant kai dookhan, and nindaa, slander, is warned against in many hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant, the holy one: shelter near good people carries you across. Today the salok's second line takes over the whole ashtpadi.

A group chat, late at night. Someone posts a screenshot of a coworker's message and adds an eye-roll. Within a minute there are six replies. Everyone has a story. Nobody is lying exactly, but by the end the coworker is a joke, and the chat has never been livelier. It feels good, in a sour sort of way. You go to sleep a little buzzed and a little worse. Guru Arjan spends an entire ashtpadi on that buzz, asking the one question the group chat never does: what is this doing to us?
screen: `A SCREENSHOT AND AN EYE-ROLL.` → `SIX REPLIES IN A MINUTE.` → `WHAT IS THIS DOING TO US?`

segments.voice: The thirteenth ashtpadi is built like a drumbeat. Line after line opens with the same three words: sant kai dookhan, through harming the holy, through speaking ill of them. Then each line names a cost. Life is cut short. All peace goes. The mind becomes dirty. Honor is lost. No one comes to help. The list runs stanza after stanza, the opening words returning like a knock on a door. Now look at who pays, in every single line. Not the sant. The good person being slandered never suffers in these stanzas. The losses all fall on the slanderer: their peace, their mind, their standing, their life. That's the surprise, and it turns the group chat upside down. We gossip because it seems to cost the other person something and give us something: a laugh, a bond, a bit of height. Sukhmani says the accounts run the other way. The one being talked about loses very little; the one talking is the one being emptied. Two words to hold. Dookhan: speaking ill, finding fault, doing harm with words. And nindaa, slander, the salok's own word. Even so, the first stanza leaves a door open: if the merciful saint shows mercy, even the slanderer is carried across in the saints' company. And why the holy, especially? Because nearness to the good lifts us, and slander pushes the good away on purpose, and with them the very company that might have carried us across.
screen: `SANT KAI DOOKHAN: A DRUMBEAT.` · `LINE AFTER LINE, A COST.` · `THE SLANDERER ALWAYS PAYS.` · `PUSHING THE GOOD AWAY.` · then, large: `SLANDER HARMS THE SLANDERER.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the mind do what it does, and when it brings up someone who annoys you and starts a little commentary, don't argue with it. Just stop the sentence halfway, like lifting a needle off a record, breathe out, and wait for the next one. You're not forcing kindness yet; you're only learning where the needle is.
Nindaa, slander. Sant kai dookhan, speaking ill of the good: in the thirteenth ashtpadi, line after line, the one who speaks is the one who pays.
Your line: slander harms the slanderer. The one talking is the one who pays. Four hundred eighty-seven days, and counting.

488.title: What slander does inside
488.hook: slander darkens the one who speaks it (Sukhmani 13)
488.howItsDone: Sikhs end the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of daily worship and many gatherings, with a line asking for sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all; Sukhmani's thirteenth ashtpadi names slander's inner stain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nindaa, slander: line after line, the one who speaks is the one who pays. Today, a look inside that speaker, and what to put there instead.

Ever notice how a complaint grows each time you tell it? The first time, it's a small thing your brother said. By the third retelling it has a beginning, a middle and a villain. You've rehearsed it so often you can feel it in your jaw. Your brother has long since forgotten. You haven't, because you've been carrying it around and polishing it. Slander works like that on the inside. It doesn't stay out there, in the story. It moves in.
screen: `A COMPLAINT GROWS EACH TELLING.` → `YOU FEEL IT IN YOUR JAW.` → `SLANDER MOVES IN.`

segments.voice: Among the thirteenth ashtpadi's costs, one goes deeper than the rest. Through slandering the holy, the text says, the mind becomes maleen: dirty, stained, like cloth dipped in mud. It's an inside cost, happening right now in the person speaking. Every time you rehearse someone's faults, you're the one marinating in them. The Guru Granth Sahib shows this from the other side, too. The poet-saint Kabir, whose hymns sit in the scripture beside the Gurus', says something startling, in paraphrase: let people slander me; slander does me good. Why? Because, in Kabir's image, the slanderer washes my dirty clothes for me. My faults move off me and onto their tongue. It's funny and a little unsettling, and it says what Sukhmani says: the dirt ends up with the one who talks. So what goes in its place? The Sikh answer is in the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of Sikh worship, which ends with sarbat da bhalaa: the good of all, the well-being of everyone, with no list of exceptions. Not my family, my side, the people I like: sarbat, all. People who say Ardas daily are wishing well, every day, to the very people they might be tempted to slander. That's the swap. Not just stopping the unkind word, which leaves an empty space, but filling it with a blessing. A stained cloth doesn't get clean by being left alone. It gets clean by being washed.

In its place, wish them one plain good thing: that they sleep well tonight, that their work goes right, that they're less worried than they seem. If you pray, you can hold them inside sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all.

489.title: Living ashtpadi 13
489.howItsDone: Gurbani returns often to the rasnaa, the tongue, and to the sweetness of speaking the Name; Sukhmani's warnings on slander and Guru Nanak's line on harsh words are read as a guard on gossip.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maleen: slander stains the speaker's mind, and sarbat da bhalaa, the good of all, washes it. Today, the thirteenth ashtpadi goes to lunch.

Try counting, for one lunch break, how much of the talk around you is about people who aren't there. Who's dating whom. Who got the promotion and didn't deserve it. What the neighbor is doing with that yard. Most of it isn't cruel. It's the easy, warm currency of being together, and that's what makes it hard: gossip usually isn't a decision. It's a habit of the tongue, running ahead of us. The thirteenth ashtpadi warned about slander of the holy. Living it means watching its smaller cousin, the one that shows up at lunch.
screen: `COUNT THE TALK AT LUNCH.` → `ABOUT PEOPLE WHO AREN'T THERE.` → `A HABIT OF THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Gurbani's word for the tongue is rasnaa, and it sits right beside ras: taste, juice, flavor. The tongue is the taster, and the Gurus play with that. What the tongue keeps tasting, it gets a taste for. Hymns speak of a tongue that savors the Name, that has found the sweetest flavor and wants nothing else. The opposite is a tongue with a taste for other people's faults, going back for more. Guru Nanak puts it bluntly in Asa di Var, the hymn we met a few days ago: speaking harsh, tasteless words, the body and mind themselves become tasteless. The word is phikaa: bland, flat, insipid, like food with no salt. Unkind talk doesn't only wound someone else; it drains the flavor out of the person talking. Put beside the thirteenth ashtpadi, the shape is clear. Slander of the holy stains the mind. Everyday gossip, its small cousin, flattens it. Both start on the tongue. So why guard the tongue rather than the thoughts? Because the tongue is where a passing thought becomes a habit. A thought about someone's faults can drift by. Said out loud, it gets an audience, a laugh, a reply, and comes back stronger tomorrow. Guarding the tongue is a gate at the end of the path: thoughts may still wander up to it, but they don't get out into the world. And a gate is a small thing to build: one changed subject, at one lunch table.

490.title: Ashtpadi 14, salok: give up cleverness
490.hook: taj siaanap: give up cleverness and remember the Lord (Sukhmani 14)
490.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the fourteenth ashtpadi with the salok beginning taj siaanap, give up cleverness, and many read it as a turn from scheming toward a single hope in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasnaa, the tongue: it learns a taste for the Name or for faults, so guard it. Today, the fourteenth ashtpadi begins.

You're in the shower, rehearsing. If I say this to my boss, then she'll say that, and then I'll mention the other thing, and that way it looks like it was her idea. Version two. Version three. The water runs, the plan gets cleverer, and somewhere around version five you notice that you're not actually solving anything. You're just circling. The fourteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with a two-word instruction for exactly that state: taj siaanap. Give up the cleverness.
screen: `IN THE SHOWER, REHEARSING.` → `VERSION TWO. VERSION FIVE.` → `TAJ SIAANAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok, in paraphrase. Give up your cleverness, good people, and remember the Lord, the King. Keep in your mind hope in the One alone. Then, Nanak, pain, doubt and fear depart. Taj: give up, let go. Siaanap: cleverness, from siaanaa, a Punjabi word that can mean wise, but also shrewd, crafty, the one who always has an angle. The salok means that second sense. Careful, because this is easy to misread. Sukhmani isn't against thinking. Guru Nanak praised the person who reflects on learning, and Sikh history is full of scholars, poets and builders. Siaanap is narrower: the scheming mind, always calculating how to come out on top, how to arrange people, how to secure every outcome in advance. Why let it go? Look at what the salok promises instead. Three things depart: dookh, pain; bharam, doubt; and bhau, fear. That's precisely the list of what the scheming mind produces. The shower plan isn't really about the boss. It's fear, wearing a clever coat. The more angles you calculate, the more angles there are to fear. The salok's alternative is simple to say and hard to do: ek aas, one hope, kept in the mind. Not a dozen backup plans, each with its own worry attached. One place to rest. The next stanzas turn to where that hope should and shouldn't rest. Today, only the first move: put the clever plan down.
screen: `TAJ: LET GO. SIAANAP: CLEVERNESS.` · `NOT THINKING, BUT SCHEMING.` · `PAIN, DOUBT AND FEAR DEPART.` · `EK AAS: ONE HOPE.` · then, large: `DROP THE CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a plan you've been circling, a conversation you keep rehearsing, an outcome you're trying to arrange, and see all its versions clearly. Then, on an out-breath, set it down; you can still act tomorrow, you're only putting down the circling. Rest in one simple hope instead of ten clever angles, and if you pray, say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Siaanap, cleverness, shrewdness. The salok says: give it up, keep one hope, and pain, doubt and fear depart.
Your line: drop the cleverness. One hope is lighter than ten angles. Four hundred ninety days now.
